title: The Trade Beneath the Forest Floor
paragraphs: Pull a fine root from a forest floor, rinse it, and set it under a microscope.
The last few millimetres are wrapped in fungal tissue or riddled with it, and that boundary is where most of the tree's mineral nutrition takes place.
The arrangement is called a mycorrhiza, and most land plant families form one.
For most trees, the organ that takes up phosphate from soil is not a root.
It is a partnership.
Botanists recognised the relationship in the 1880s, reinterpreting the pale sheath on pine and beech root tips as a partner rather than an infection.
Plant remains roughly four hundred million years old contain branched structures resembling the feeding organs modern fungi build inside plant cells.
The symbiosis looks about as old as land plants themselves; plants seem to have reached dry ground with fungi rather than recruiting them later.
Two associations dominate.
In an arbuscular mycorrhiza the fungus breaches the wall of a cortex cell and grows inside it, branching into a shape like a miniature tree.
That structure is the arbuscule, the exchange surface.
The plant cell does not simply give way.
Its own membrane stretches inward around every branch, so the two organisms stay separated by two membranes and never share cytoplasm.
Other hyphae swell into vesicles that store lipid.
An ectomycorrhiza never enters a living cell.
The fungus instead sheathes the root tip in a dense mantle of hyphae, then pushes a lattice of flattened hyphae between the outer root cells.
That lattice is the Hartig net, and it does the arbuscule's job by wrapping cells rather than entering them.
Thousands of fungal species form ectomycorrhizas, and many are the familiar mushrooms of forest floors: boletes, amanitas, chanterelles and truffles.
Only about two percent of seed plant species take this route, but they include the pines, oaks, beeches and birches that build most of the world's forests.
The reason a tree pays for either arrangement comes down to geometry and to one stubborn nutrient.
Phosphate barely moves in soil.
It binds to mineral surfaces and diffuses so slowly that a root strips the millimetre or two around itself within days, then sits in its own depletion zone.
A fine root is perhaps two to five hundred micrometres across and a root hair ten to twenty.
A fungal hypha is two to ten micrometres across, finds purchase in pores far too narrow for a root hair to enter, and extends centimetres past the depleted shell.
Per unit of carbon spent, hyphae buy far more absorbing surface than roots do.
What travels back is, above all, phosphate, strung into chains called polyphosphate for the journey and released at the exchange interface.
Nitrogen moves too, as ammonium and as amino acids.

Many ectomycorrhizal fungi secrete enzymes that break down protein in leaf litter, which lets their trees tap nitrogen locked inside dead tissue, while arbuscular fungi rely on nitrogen already freed into the soil.
The plant pays in carbon, and it pays twice over.
Sugar crosses the interface as simple six carbon units.
Lipid crosses as well, which is the more surprising half of the bill.

Arbuscular fungi cannot manufacture their own fatty acids and must be handed them by a host, which is largely why no one could grow one to completion on a plate without a plant until a fatty acid was supplied directly.
That bill is not trivial.
Estimates of the share of a plant's photosynthetic output that ends up in fungal partners run from four to twenty percent, highest in seedlings and poor soils.
Experiments that sever the phloem by girdling a trunk show the flow falling away within days, which means the fungi live on sugar made that week, not on stored reserves.
A colonised root system is a powerful sink, and sugar made up in the leaves is drawn down to it rather than kept in the shoot.
The obvious question is where the carbon ends up, and the tool that answers it is the labelled atom.
Seal a seedling in a bag, feed it carbon dioxide built from an uncommon isotope, and every sugar it makes for the next several hours carries a tag instruments can detect at very low concentrations.
Wait, then harvest the plants nearby and look for the tag.
Separating the fungal route from the soil takes a second trick.
Investigators grow donor and receiver in compartments divided by a mesh whose pores admit hyphae but exclude roots, and sometimes rotate the mesh cylinder to shear any hyphae that cross.
Run these designs and labelled carbon does turn up in neighbouring plants, across species as well as within them, and shaded receivers often show more than sunlit ones.
This is the point where care is required, because a tag in a neighbour is not automatically carbon in a neighbour.
Much of what the instruments detect sits in hyphae wrapped around and threaded through the receiving root, which is fungal tissue, not plant tissue.

The stricter tests look for the tag above ground, in stem and leaves, and by that measure the quantity that clearly crosses into plant tissue is usually a small fraction of what the receiver fixes for itself.
The network is also not the only road.

Labelled carbon can leak from roots into soil water and be taken up by a neighbour, be respired underground as carbon dioxide and fixed again above ground, travel in fallen litter, or cross a graft where two roots have fused.
Each of these is real, none requires a fungal conduit, and pulling them apart in a forest rather than a pot is genuinely difficult.
Suppose all of that is handled and real transfer is shown.
A further claim is smuggled in when the result is described as one tree feeding another, because purpose is a separate question from movement.

The fungus is not an inert pipe but a third organism with an interest of its own, usually joined to many hosts at once, and it can hold carbon in its hyphae, spend it exploring new soil, or pour it into spores.
Flow may be set by the fungus, or simply by which end of the connection is hungrier.
Evolution sharpens the objection.

Natural selection acts on the donor, and a trait that costs a tree carbon while benefiting a competitor should be whittled down over generations unless the donor gets something back: a better fungal partner, a return flow later, or the survival of a relative.
No such account is needed for leakage down a gradient, which happens whenever a tissue rich in sugar is plumbed to one short of it.
The plain explanation is the one to beat.
One group of plants shows how far the conduit can go.
Ghost pipe and a number of orchids carry no usable chlorophyll and make no sugar at all.
They live on carbon drawn from fungi attached at the same time to photosynthetic trees, as clear a demonstration as anyone could want that plant carbon can cross a fungus into another plant.
It also cuts the other way.
These plants return nothing.
The route says nothing about generosity at either end.
That distinction has largely been lost outside the laboratory.
The image of the forest as a web of nurture, old trees knowingly provisioning seedlings and warnings passing from root to root, has become the standard telling, and the appeal is easy to see.
Some of it is defensible as metaphor.

But the confident language of intention has run well ahead of the measurements, and recent surveys have found that several of the most repeated claims rest on a handful of studies, and that sources cited for the strongest statements often do not say what those statements report.
None of this diminishes the science.
What is not in doubt is plain enough: the symbiosis is ancient, nearly universal, and structurally elegant.
The trade of mineral nutrients for sugar and fat is measured and quantified.
Carbon does move through fungal tissue between root systems.
What stays open is how much of that movement matters to a growing forest, and whether anything resembling provisioning happens at all.
The gap is where the interesting work sits, and a bargain that old was never going to need the decoration.
